india-f7de735a1e.headline: India GDP grows 7.8%, but PM Modi urges less gold purchase, foreign travel: Does it help the economy? Expert weighs in
india-f7de735a1e.fulltext:
Sayantani Biswas Published5 Sep 2026, 11:17 PM IST India's economy grew 7.8% in the first quarter of fiscal 2026-27, beating expectations despite higher oil prices and global supply-chain disruptions. At the same time, the government has renewed its call for Indians to curb non-essential foreign travel, overseas weddings and gold purchases, bringing attention to how household spending affects the wider economy. Prime Minister Narendra Modi made the appeal on September 1 in a video posted on Instagram from the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Bishkek, linking domestic spending choices with India's goal of becoming a developed economy by 2047. "Foreign trips, if you are going for leisure, you should not go. If you are getting married abroad, you should not do so. And if it is not necessary, you should not buy gold either." Data from the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation showed that real GDP stood at ₹81.36 lakh crore in Q1 FY27, compared with ₹75.46 lakh crore a year earlier. The 7.8% expansion exceeded the Reserve Bank of India's projection of around 7% and followed revised growth of 8.6% in the previous quarter. The strong performance came despite external pressures, including oil price volatility and disruptions to global supply chains. The latest figures have also brought renewed attention to the composition of India's economic activity and the way household spending contributes to growth. Gold has a distinctive role in the Indian economy. It is widely held as jewellery, savings and an investment, making it an important component of household wealth. At the same time, India imports most of the gold it consumes. Strong demand therefore results in an outflow of foreign exchange and can affect the country's external balance. This is why policymakers have periodically encouraged households to avoid unnecessary gold purchases and instead consider domestic financial assets and other forms of investment. But gold has another connection to GDP that makes the issue more complicated. Gold does not simply represent money leaving the country. In national accounting, purchases of valuables such as gold can contribute to measured economic activity. Economists have previously highlighted periods when a surge in gold buying contributed to headline GDP growth without necessarily generating productive investment. In 2015, for instance, estimates suggested that India's growth rate would have been 6.34% rather than 7.4% if spending on valuables and discrepancies were excluded. Gold-related expenditure had risen 45% year on year during that quarter. The distinction is important. A purchase can contribute to measured economic activity while doing little to expand the economy's productive capacity. Overseas holidays and weddings present a different version of the same issue. Money spent on hotels, venues, travel and other services abroad represents consumption by Indian residents but does not directly generate demand for businesses operating within India. Encouraging consumers to spend that money domestically is therefore part of the broader swadeshi and self-reliance push. However, the appeal is aimed at changing consumer behaviour rather than introducing a new restriction on foreign travel or overseas weddings. Oil imports and volatile capital flows remain bigger swing factors for India's external balance — foreign portfolio investors have pulled nearly $30 billion out of Indian equities in 2026. But, economic expert, Dr Sujan Hajra says gold and travel spending is still "far too large to dismiss as macroeconomically insignificant," and doubts the timing of the appeal, a day after the GDP print, is coincidental. The backdrop: forex reserves slipped from about $728 billion in February 2026 to around $691 billion by May, as an Iran-linked oil spike pushed Brent toward $105 a barrel, with the current account deficit estimated near $84 billion for the year. India imported roughly 721 tonnes of gold worth nearly $72 billion in FY26, a record value driven by prices, not volumes. Travel adds another large bill: with airfares included, Dr Hajra puts the total at $47-50 billion ( ₹4-4.5 lakh crore) for about 33 million outbound travellers in 2025. Together, the two amount to "something approaching $120 billion of annual forex demand — in the same broad range as India's entire oil import bill." A 10% moderation could cut forex demand by about $12 billion, roughly 0.3% of GDP — not enough to alter India's growth trajectory, Dr Hajra says, "but meaningful for the current account and the rupee." If households skip the gold and the trip, does the money disappear? "In most plausible cases it does not," says Dr Hajra. Travel is the clearest case: shifted to domestic tourism, "the spending still happens — it just goes to Indian airlines, hotels, restaurants, taxis and retail instead," cutting forex leakage while lifting domestic demand and jobs. Gold works differently, since it is as much saving as consumption. Redirected into deposits, mutual funds, equities or bonds, "national saving doesn't decline — its composition changes," with money once idle as $72 billion of gold instead financing businesses, housing and infrastructure. Dr Hajra doesn't overstate this: some money will go to other consumption, some will simply be saved — but even bank deposits get intermediated into credit. He also rejects reading the appeal as austerity, noting it was paired with a "wed in India" push rather than a call to spend less. The real argument, he says, is about "changing the composition of household expenditure and saving... toward domestic consumption and financial savings." The debate is ultimately less about whether Indians should buy gold or travel abroad and more about where economic demand is being directed. India's 7.8% quarterly growth shows strong economic momentum. But policymakers are also seeking to ensure that rising household purchasing power supports domestic production, investment and employment rather than increasing demand for imported goods and overseas services. That creates a broader question for India's growth story: as incomes rise, can a greater share of consumption be channelled towards activities that strengthen domestic productive capacity while reducing pressure on the country's external finances? Sayantani Biswas Sayantani Biswas is an assistant editor at Livemint with seven years of experience covering geopolitics, foreign policy, international relations and global power dynamics. She reports on Indian and international politics, including elections worldwide, and specialises in historically grounded analysis of contemporary conflicts and state decisions. She joined Mint in 2021, after covering politics at publications including The Telegraph.
She holds an MPhil in Comparative Literature from Jadavpur University (2019), with a specialisation in postcolonial Latin American literature. Her research examined economic nationalism through Eduardo Galeano’s Open Veins of Latin America. She also writes on political language, cultural memory and the long shadows of conflict.
Biswas grew up in Durgapur, an industrial town in West Bengal shaped by migration, which drew families from across India to the Durgapur Steel Plant. As the only child in a joint family, she spent years listening—almost obsessively—to her grandparents’ testimonies of struggle, fear and loss as they fled Bangladesh during the Partition of 1947. This formative exposure to lived historical memory later converged with her training in Comparative Literature, equipping her to analyse socio-economic structures and their reverberations.
Outside the newsroom, she gravitates towards cultural history and critical theory, returning often to texts such as Paulo Freire’s Pedagogy of the Oppressed. As a journalist, she is committed to accuracy, intellectual rigour and fairness, and believes political reporting demands not only clarity and speed, but historical depth, contextual precision, and a disciplined resistance to spectacle. ai-1bbdfbbe4f.headline: Tatas HyperVault to build India’s Largest 1GW AI Data Centre in Hyderabad
ai-1bbdfbbe4f.fulltext:
TCS to Build India's Largest Data Centre in Hyderabad by 2028
Telangana Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy, in a meeting with officials from TCS’ HyperVault, called the project ‘historic’ not just for Telangana but for India.
Hyderabad: Telangana will host the country’s largest AI data centre campus, with TCS subsidiary HyperVault and its partners investing up to ₹70,000 crore in a one gigawatt (1,000 megawtt) facility spread over more than 250 acres in Future City. This is the largest single investment in the state’s AI and data-centre infrastructure sector. The project is expected to create around 7,000 direct and indirect jobs and is planned to be inaugurated on June 2, 2028, on the occasion of Telangana Formation Day.
Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy announced the mega investment after a meeting with senior representatives of Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) and HyperVault here on Saturday, during which the government and the company signed a memorandum of understanding for developing the campus. Setting a firm deadline, Revanth Reddy said the government wanted the country’s largest AI data centre to be inaugurated exactly 21 months from Saturday, on June 2, 2028, Telangana Formation Day
“This is a historic project not just for Telangana but for India,” the Chief Minister said, describing the announcement as one of the biggest investments in artificial intelligence (AI) and Future City. He said Hyderabad was now at the forefront of the global AI revolution and that access to AI models and computing capacity was rapidly becoming a form of public infrastructure. Having such computing capacity located in Telangana, he said, would provide the state with a significant strategic advantage.
The Chief Minister also highlighted the 50-km Radial Road-1, connecting the Outer Ring Road with Future City through Kongarakalan, saying it would be among the best roads in India and could potentially serve as an emergency runway. He said the road had been dedicated to Bharat Ratna Ratan Tata, recalling his announcement at the Telangana Rising Global Summit 2025 that a major road would be dedicated to an organisation investing ₹1 lakh crore in Telangana.
TCS CEO K. Krithivasan, COO Aarthi Subramanian, HyperVault president V. Rajanna and HyperVault CEO and managing director Deepesh Nanda participated in the meeting. OpenAI chief technology officer Uday Rudraraju joined through videoconference from the United States. IT and industries Minister D. Sridhar Babu, ministers N. Uttam Kumar Reddy, Komatireddy Venkat Reddy and Adluri Laxman Kumar, Chief Secretary Sanjay Jaju and government adviser K. Ramakrishna Rao were among those present.
Recalling his meeting with Tata Sons Chairman N. Chandrasekaran at the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, Revanth Reddy said he had asked Chandrasekaran to bring “big news” for Telangana in terms of investment. “He smiled and accepted. He promised me that he would announce it shortly,” the Chief Minister said. He explained that the state government had deliberately refrained from announcing the investment until the Tata Group formally made the announcement.
Revanth Reddy also sought to assure investors that Telangana would maintain policy continuity irrespective of changes in government. Referring to the investment policies followed by successive governments in undivided Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, he said governments had improved existing policies rather than abandoning them.
“There is no policy paralysis in my state. I don’t want to create any confusion. I want to give you more and more confidence and political differences and ideological differences will not affect the investments policy,” he said.
Krithivasan described AI as not merely a technology disruption but a “civilisational shift” that would transform the way societies function. Countries and societies that successfully transition to AI, he said, would be at the forefront, while India had a major opportunity to catch up. He said HyperVault advanced TCS’s “Infrastructure-to-Intelligence” strategy by combining AI-ready infrastructure with its cloud, engineering, enterprise transformation and AI capabilities.
1,000-MW (1-GW) AI data centre campus, with TCS subsidiary HyperVault and partners investing up to ₹70,000 crore. to come up on 250 acres in Future City.
Facility to provide high-end, AI-ready computing infrastructure for frontier AI companies, global hyperscalers and enterprises.
It will incorporate high-performance computing systems, high-density power infrastructure and advanced liquid-cooling technologies.
At full build-out, the campus is expected to rank among the largest and most advanced AI infrastructure campuses in India.
Campus will be developed using green energy and water-neutral design principles.
Government says project would strengthen Telangana’s position as a strategic destination for AI and advanced digital infrastructure.

indian-startups-0db2a9f550.headline: KRAFTON To Invest $250 Mn In Indian AI & Deeptech Startups
indian-startups-0db2a9f550.fulltext: Doubling down on India, South Korean gaming giant KRAFTON plans to invest an additional $250 Mn (₹3,300 Cr) in Indian startups over the next three to four years. Beyond gaming, KRAFTON said that the new corpus will expand its focus to emerging areas such as artificial intelligence (AI), robotics, deeptech, among others. This is in addition to the $250 Mn that the gaming giant has already invested in the country, taking its total planned investment in India to $500 Mn (₹6,600 Cr). Separately, KRAFTON, in partnership with Mirae Asset Global Investments and NAVER, had also launched a $670 Mn (₹6,000 Cr) venture fund to back Indian startups last year. The announcement came as KRAFTON chairman Byung Gyu Chang met Prime Minister Narendra Modi in New Delhi today. In a statement, the company said that Chang, during the meeting, reaffirmed KRAFTON’s commitment to India and its rapidly growing gaming, technology and digital entertainment ecosystem. The two also discussed opportunities for India and the Republic of Korea to work closely in areas of gaming, innovation and emerging technologies. “... Through our investments, skill-development initiatives and focus on emerging technologies, we look forward to working alongside India’s growing community of creators, developers and entrepreneurs to build globally relevant experiences and technologies,” added Chang. The BGMI maker has been making investments in India since March 2021. Its India portfolio counts the likes of names such as esports startup NODWIN, streaming platform Loco and self-publishing platform Pratilipi. It also acquired a controlling 75% stake in Pune-based gaming studio Nautilus Mobile last year. Besides investments, India is also a key market for KRAFTON given the country’s high smartphone penetration and ease of access to digital payments, which enable micro transactions. The South Korean gaming giant’s flagship product is Battlegrounds Mobile India (BGMI), formerly known as PUBG, which has surpassed 260 Mn downloads in the country. KRAFTON is expanding its investment focus in India as the ban on real-money gaming (RMG) last year suffered a big blow to the local ecosystem. Many big names have either crumbled since then or pivoted to new business models, while early stage funding activity has remained tepid for the sector. As a result, KRAFTON likely sees deeptech and AI as the next big frontier for its investments in India. And it is not without reason. Buoyed by policy clarity, government sops, capital inflows, growing demand and brewing investor confidence, Indian AI startups raised $676 Mn during the first six months of 2026. As per Inc42 data, India’s AI economy is projected to become a $126 Bn opportunity by 2030.

other-interests-189e84f107.headline: Fermat’s last theorem formalised by AI agents in just 11 days
other-interests-189e84f107.fulltext:
AI company Anthropic has created a formalised proof of Fermat’s last theorem. It took just 11 days for a group of AI agents to complete the task, confirming that the human-found proof proposed in the 1990s is correct.
Fermat’s last theorem puzzled mathematicians for centuries until it was proved in 1995 by Andrew Wiles. It states that there are no whole numbers a, b, and c that satisfy the equation aⁿ + bⁿ = cⁿ, where n is a whole number greater than 2.
The theorem, though easy to state, was fiendishly difficult to prove. Mathematician Pierre de Fermat posed the puzzle in the 17th century and famously alluded to a proof that he claimed to have discovered, saying that it was too large to fit in the margins of the textbook he was writing in.
Advertisement
Many mathematicians tried and failed to find a proof. Wiles worked on the problem for seven years in secret before announcing his breakthrough in 1993. Proofs often involve lengthy logical arguments that build on each other. If a single step contains an error, then the whole thing can collapse. This happened to Wiles when a flaw was found in his proof, which took him and collaborator Richard Taylor around a year to fix.
Formalising mathematical theorems is a solution to this problem. It takes them out of the realm of pen and paper, and puts them into a configuration – computer code – that allows machines to grapple with them, methodically working through the logic and exposing any flaws. There are already 2 million lines of formalised mathematics stored in a central repository called Mathlib.
Earlier this year, a conference of AI experts, computer scientists and mathematicians was held in London by Kevin Buzzard at Imperial College London, who was – until Anthropic’s announcement – working on a five-year project to formalise Wiles and Taylor’s 100-page proof in a programming language called Lean, so that it can be formally checked for correctness and used as a foundation for further research.
Buzzard said at the time that when his project began he was confident of success, but that recent advances in AI had convinced him that the project would be complete much faster than he previously thought possible. Anthropic’s announcement has now overtaken that effort and wrapped up the problem.
Buzzard said in a statement published by Anthropic that the company’s proof leaves “no assumptions other than the axioms of mathematics”. In short, the problem is solved.
“Along the way we see autoformalisation of algebra, harmonic analysis, geometry and number theory, and we learn that AI autoformalisation artefacts are now robust enough to be built upon; the proof is multi-layered,” said Buzzard. “If the automatic formalisation of FLT is possible now, then we have taken a big step towards automatic formalisation of the modern mathematical literature.”
In its blog post announcing the result, Anthropic wrote that its Claude model worked continuously and autonomously for 11 days to write the proof. Numerous separate AI agents were involved, with different tasks, like tackling smaller chunks of the theorem, being assigned to each.
Human experts occasionally issued “high-level instructions” to keep the work on track, the company says. Several times, the agents “lost track of the project’s state and stopped collaborating effectively”. Interestingly, the company said that success came after it began using a tool designed for human mathematical collaboration called Prove2Me, which helped different agents track their work and decide on next tasks.
Anthropic’s formalisation runs to 13 million lines of Lean and covers roughly 29,500 intermediate theorems that were necessary stepping stones towards completing the overall work. That makes the proof over five times the current size of all previous work on Mathlib, which also makes it the largest Lean proof ever written.

india-0a5eb086d7.headline: China to proceed with Brahmaputra mega dam despite new concerns
india-0a5eb086d7.source: India Latest News: Top National Headlines Today & Breaking News | The Hindu
india-0a5eb086d7.fulltext:
Fresh concerns triggered by the devastating glacial collapse along the Nepal-China border are unlikely to sway Beijing's plans to go ahead with the construction of a mega dam on the lower reaches of the Yarlung Zangbo, or the Brahmaputra River, in a seismically active region in Tibet near the border with India.
On July 23, 2026, a month before the August 26 flash flood and mudslides, China released its 15th Five-Year Plan for renewable energy, which called for advancing the construction of major projects, including the Yarlung Zangbo Lower Reaches Hydropower Project, as the mega dam project is referred to in China.
Underscoring the importance accorded to the plan, China’s Vice Premier Zhang Guoqing visited Nyingchi in Tibet, near the border, in April this year. "We must shoulder the principal responsibility for project‑building and build this landmark mega project of the new era,” he was quoted as saying, adding that the government would “put quality first, safety as the foundation, strictly enforce construction standards and ecological‑environmental‑protection requirements, and keep construction progress subordinate to quality and safety.”
‘Project of the century’
At a groundbreaking ceremony in July 2025, China’s second-ranked leader and Premier Li Qiang, who travelled to Nyingchi, announced the start of construction of what he called “the project of the century”. A total investment of 1.2 trillion Yuan (around ₹14 lakh crore) was announced for the construction of five power stations.
Since then, there has been little public information about the project, although Mr. Zhang’s visit this year shed some light on how the project will go forward, including the setting up of the new State-run China Yajiang Group to run the entire project, which he inspected.
China has already opened one major dam on the middle reaches of the Yarlung Zangbo at Zangmu. A State media report earlier this month lauded the construction of the dam, saying it had “provided a solution to nearly 26 percent of electricity demand in Southwest China’s Xizang [Tibet] Autonomous Region”, the report said, detailing an elaborate “fishway” designed to help fish move between upstream and downstream sections. The report quoted design engineer Zhang Lianming as saying the fishway would likely be used for future projects.
In June this year, a “final acceptance meeting” of the Zangmu project was held, declaring that the dam, which started construction in 2010, had generated 22.2 billion kilowatt-hours of energy “equivalent to saving approximately 7.4 million tonnes of standard coal and cutting carbon dioxide emissions by around 22.2 million tonnes”.
The energy generation of the new project near the India border, where the course of the Yarlung Zangbo stunningly falls over the “great bend” and turns towards India, is expected to easily dwarf Zangmu.
While there have been no official projections, Chinese analysts project 60 GW installed capacity and 300 billion kilowatt-hours of power a year, more than three times the Three Gorges.
While the project has been described as a “run-of-the-river” dam, it will also involve the construction of a reservoir. This is likely to be located in the town of Mainling, upstream of Nyingchi, a prefecture-level city that is also home to a key airport, according to an analysis published on Wednesday by David Fishman, a Shanghai-based analyst writing on energy who looked at reports of relocations to ascertain the likely location. The water will be diverted at the top of the great bend into an approximately 40-km-long tunnel, Mr. Fishman wrote on his Substack, “Crossing the River”, as its descending force powers five 12-GW powerhouses before rejoining the river.
India’s concerns
Of concern to India is how much water is likely to be stored in the reservoir and how the tunnel will affect downstream flows, as well as possible broader ecological impacts. The lack of information has posed an obstacle in assessing the possible impact.
Later this month, India and China will hold a meeting of the Expert-Level Mechanism on Trans-border Rivers. However, the sharing of hydrological data, officials say, has not been regular and has on occasion been suspended during difficult periods in relations.
Asked about the project, China’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said last year that Beijing “always maintained a highly responsible attitude toward transboundary river development and has rich experience in hydropower project development”. He said the “construction of the project is beneficial for disaster prevention and mitigation throughout the entire river basin and will not have adverse effects on downstream areas”.
“China has conducted hydrological reporting, flood control, and disaster reduction cooperation with relevant downstream countries and has also engaged in necessary communication regarding the project,” he said.

world-83f9a270e2.headline: US envoys meet Putin in Moscow for Ukraine talks
world-83f9a270e2.fulltext:
US envoys meet Putin in Moscow for Ukraine talks
- Published
US President Donald Trump's top negotiators have met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, as efforts to end the war in Ukraine gather pace.
Footage released by the Kremlin showed Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner being greeted by Putin, who said the current situation "is not so easy".
Witkoff thanked Putin for agreeing with Ukraine to halt strikes on each other's capitals for three days. On Sunday the envoys will travel to Kyiv for more talks - their first such visit to Ukraine's capital.
On Friday, Trump said Witkoff and Kushner were "bringing with them a proposal to end the war". So far, efforts by the US and its allies to broker a peace deal have failed.
At Saturday's talks in the Kremlin, Putin also said that "whatever happens, such contacts are undoubtedly always useful". He also thanked Trump for his peacemaking efforts.
He told the envoys that he was "comfortable" working with them, adding: "Of course on our side there is quite a high level of trust during this work."
The talks – held behind closed doors in Putin's official residence in the heart of the Russian capital – lasted for three hours, according to Russian state media.
Details are still emerging, but Putin adviser Yuri Ushakov described the talks as "constructive, extremely frank".
"The talks were not limited to an exchange of views on resolving the Ukrainian crisis - economic issues and potential major, mutually beneficial Russian-American projects were discussed in considerable detail," he said.
Ushakov also said "note was made of the Russian army's tangible advances in the combat zone" and that there was acknowledgement that talks needed to address "the root causes of the conflict".
Despite an escalation of Russian missile and drone strikes on Ukrainian cities including Kyiv, Russian ground forces have made very slow advances for most of the conflict, incurring enormous casualties. Russia still controls about one-fifth of Ukrainian territory - areas that it seized back in 2022.
Zelensky said earlier on Saturday that he had spoken to the envoys, who have "already begun working with the Russian side today".
"The plan for tomorrow's diplomatic engagements in Kyiv, involving the US team, has been approved. We are waiting for Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and are ready for a substantive conversation," he added.
"From now through the end of Saturday, as well as on Sunday and Monday, Ukraine is ready to refrain from strikes on Moscow, and we expect the Russians to do the same regarding Kyiv."
Russian state media reported that Putin had ordered a halt to strikes on Kyiv for three days due to the US visit.
In televised remarks, Putin said Russia had not agreed to a ceasefire for the rest of Ukraine outside of the capital.
The Russian president said he would "ensure the security of the negotiating process" and of the mediators.
Kushner and Witkoff have visited Russia several times but the talks on Sunday would be the first in Ukraine. It is not clear how the US envoys will be travelling from Moscow to Kyiv.
Ukraine's airspace has been closed since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Delegations from Ukraine have attended talks in the US over the past 18 months.
Earlier on Saturday, Zelensky said Russia had fired "demonstrative" strikes on airports in Kyiv and Boryspil overnight ahead of his planned meeting with the US.
Ukraine's president added: "Clearly, these Russian strikes on the airports are a reaction to the discussions and preparations for the possibility of the US side using an aircraft to travel to Ukraine and land at Kyiv Airport or Boryspil Airport."
Zelensky said on Friday he would guarantee the safety of Russian airspace during the envoys' visit and called for Russia to do the same for Ukraine.
He also said an overnight Russian strike on a civilian building in the Dnipro region killed four people and injured five others.
Witkoff and Kushner's visit to Moscow comes just over a week after a rare visit to the Russian capital by the head of the CIA, John Ratcliffe.
There was no official comment from Washington or the Kremlin on what was discussed. Speaking last week, Trump described the meeting as "semi-routine".
Last year, the US, Ukraine and Russia separately suggested that a deal to end the war was edging closer following a flurry of talks brokered by the Americans.
European allies also held talks in Paris but discussions ultimately ended without a breakthrough. Key disagreements remain between the warring sides on issues such as territory and security guarantees for Ukraine.
In recent months, both Russia and Ukraine have intensified their aerial attacks as fighting continues.
Ukraine said it has struggled to repel ballistic missile attacks due to a lack of interceptor missiles, while Kyiv has focused its strikes on Russian economic infrastructure targets.

india-da4858c5ee.headline: PM Modi holds talks with Russian Prez Putin, focusing on trade, energy & defence; says India backs every effort to end war in Ukraine | Akashvani News
india-da4858c5ee.fulltext:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi today held talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the 26th annual Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in the capital city of Kyrgyzstan, Bishkek. The discussions focused on key areas of India-Russia bilateral cooperation, including trade and investment, energy and defence.
During the meeting, Prime Minister Modi said it was a matter of deep satisfaction that cooperation between India and Russia continued to scale new heights. 
On the Ukraine conflict, PM Modi stressed the need for a peaceful resolution, saying that every day of war sets humanity back. He told President Putin that resolving all issues through peaceful means is a call of humanity. PM Modi said, ” We must move from endless wars to ending wars,’ adding that India supports all efforts towards peace.
The meeting took place more than a week before President Putin is scheduled to travel to India to attend the annual BRICS summit.
During the meeting, the Prime Minister said India is hosting the BRICS Summit in a few days, and all Indians are eager to welcome Mr Putin and his delegation. He said the visit of the Russian President will strengthen bilateral relations and further reinforce dialogue and cooperation within the BRICS framework.
President Vladimir Putin showed his satisfaction that Indian-Russian relations continue to strengthen on the basis of the principles of a special and privileged partnership.

ai-5e91c57873.headline: US-based tech giant Adobe acquires Indian AI startup Rilo less than a year after launch
ai-5e91c57873.fulltext:
Adobe has acquired Indian AI startup Rilo, less than a year after its launch, as the US software company expands its capabilities in AI-powered marketing automation.
Adobe confirmed the acquisition but has not provided further details about the deal.
The transaction is Adobe's second known acquisition of an Indian startup, following its purchase of Bengaluru-based generative AI video company Rephrase.ai in 2023.
Rilo was founded in September 2025 by IIT Bombay batchmates Dhruv Jaglan and Georgi Boby. The startup developed an AI automation platform aimed at marketing and go-to-market teams.
Its technology allowed users to describe workflows in plain English and have AI agents build and execute them across different tools. Rilo supported tasks including competitor intelligence, prospecting, content repurposing and distribution, sales-call analysis and campaign research.
The platform also allowed customers to create their own customised AI workflows rather than relying only on pre-built automations.
Jaglan said more than 10,000 users had built with Rilo within months of its launch.
Announcing the acquisition on LinkedIn, he said Rilo was joining Adobe to help bring AI to Fortune 500 marketers. He said the company had started with the aim of expanding the use of AI among knowledge workers beyond engineers.
Boby also confirmed the deal on LinkedIn, saying Rilo's mission from the beginning had been to expand the power of AI beyond engineers.
“I'm incredibly proud of the team, what we've built and the pace we built it in,” he wrote, adding that the move to Adobe would allow the team to continue that mission at a larger scale.
According to media reports, Rilo raised $1 million from investors including Peak XV Partners, DeVC and Day Zero Ventures at a valuation of $10 million.
As part of the deal, Adobe is expected to integrate some of Rilo's intellectual property and bring its six-member team on board. Rilo's investors are also expected to receive an exit.
Rahul Gupta, managing partner at Day Zero Ventures, described Rilo's workflow builder as being ahead of the curve and said it could be valuable to Adobe in enhancing customer experience and productivity.
Rilo will shut down following the acquisition, and its platform will no longer be available to customers. Jaglan said the company will help users move their workflows during the transition.
Adobe has not publicly detailed where Rilo's technology will be incorporated into its products.
The acquisition comes as technology companies increasingly use AI agents to automate marketing workflows, from content production and distribution to customer engagement and campaign analysis.

ai-5d4986f08b.headline: OpenAI confirms ‘wiki incident,’ says it’s ‘working on a framework’ for more disclosure
ai-5d4986f08b.fulltext:
OpenAI has acknowledged its role in a recently reported incident where AI agents took over a German wiki forum. The company also said it’s “past time” to “define standards” around how it shares information around incidents where its technology behaves in unexpected ways.
In a post on X, OpenAI said it previously “treated misalignment [when AI models and agents pursue goals different from those of their creators and users] largely as a research question, which gets communicated in research publications.” But as misalignment has “caused new types of real-world impact,” the company said its approach needs “to expand for this new phase of model capabilities.”
On Friday, Reuters reported that OpenAI agents had escaped from their testing environment and “hijacked” an obscure German wiki forum, turning it into a message board for other agents. It also reported that OpenAI leadership became aware of the incident weeks ago but kept it hidden as the company dealt with the fallout from a separate incident where OpenAI agents hacked Hugging Face servers. (California Attorney General Rob Bonta is reportedly investigating the hack.)
A company spokesperson told Reuters that OpenAI could not “meaningfully respond to claims or findings on a report that we have not had an opportunity to review,” but they insisted that the company’s legal team had not discouraged an investigation.
In its more recent social media post, OpenAI said it had considered the “wiki incident” to be “an instance of misalignment similar” to others that it had already shared. The company contrasted this with “the Hugging Face incident,” where it “followed a traditional security incident response playbook.”
During a media briefing this week, Jacob Steinhardt, founder and CEO of nonprofit research lab Transluce, told reporters that the tools being developed and tested by AI labs are “fundamentally difficult to control and have significant risk of leaking out of the lab.” So Steinhardt argued, “We need to hold this technology to at least the same standards we hold other high-risk scientific research to.”
OpenAI’s statement also gestured at the need for more standards, stating that both OpenAI and “the larger AI community do not yet have a clear standard for how to report misalignment that shows up during training, evaluation, and deployment, including examples that don’t look like traditional security incidents but could provide insight into AI behavior and future risks.”
In the absence of that standard, OpenAI said it’s “working on a framework and will share it in upcoming weeks, and in parallel we’re working with dozens of government regulatory agencies worldwide on these issues.”
OpenAI isn’t the only AI company dealing with these issues, as both Meta and Anthropic have acknowledged incidents where their agents misbehaved.

ai-266031deb4.headline: XDOF, just three months out of stealth, is in talks for a Series B at a $1.2B valuation
ai-266031deb4.fulltext:
Less than three months after emerging from stealth, XDOF, a startup that collects real-world teleoperation data for training general-purpose robots, is in late-stage talks to raise a Series B at a valuation of about $1.2 billion valuation led by 8VC, several people with knowledge of the deal said.
XDOF was co-founded by UC Berkeley researchers Philipp Wu (CEO) and Fred Shentu (CTO) in 2024. TechCrunch reported on the startup’s $70 million Series A in June, with participation from Thrive Capital, Andreessen Horowitz, Lux, and Spark Capital. XDOF wasn’t planning to raise again so soon after that round. But the company’s rapid growth — with annualized revenue approaching $50 million — prompted VCs to approach it about a new round, the people said.
TechCrunch was unable to learn the total capital being raised or whether the valuation includes the new funding. The terms of the deal are not final and could still change.
XDOF and 8VC didn’t respond to our request for comment.
The startup aims to build the data pipelines, collection tools, and annotation systems that frontier AI labs and robotics companies can’t easily build themselves, essentially acting as an outsourced data-supply chain for the robotics industry.
As a PhD student, Wu was studying how robots learn from large datasets. One big impediment to his research was the lack of “large-scale data to work with,” he told TechCrunch in June.
So he teamed up with Shentu on a project called GELLO, a low-cost teleoperation system that allows a human operator to control a robotic arm remotely in order to generate training data. Their work led to an influential paper in robotics.
That research formed the foundation for XDOF, which investors now describe as the Scale AI or Mercor for physical robotics, a reference to the data-labeling giants that helped fuel the AI boom. Unlike LLMs, which initially trained on the entirety of the internet, physical robots don’t have an equivalent real-world dataset to draw from, making data collection a critical bottleneck to building general-purpose machines.
XDOF is partnering with UC Berkeley’s AI Research lab to release what it believes is the largest collection of high-quality robot training data ever assembled, dubbed ABC.
To capture this data, XDOF combines remote robot teleoperation with human collectors who wear sensors to record everyday tasks like folding clothes and flattening boxes.
The startup plans to hire and train teams of data collectors worldwide, including teleoperators who steer robots remotely and egocentric operators who wear body sensors to capture movement data.
XDOF previously told TechCrunch that it is already working with 20 customers, including several frontier AI labs.
Other startups attempting to collect real-world data for robot training include Mecka AI, as well as human-data platforms expanding beyond LLMs, such as Scale AI and Micro1.

deep-tech-c33c8a67cb.headline: US seeks a cheaper alternative to MQ-9 as India seeks these drones for USD 3 billion
deep-tech-c33c8a67cb.fulltext:
The US Air Force wants a cheaper and faster replacement for its dwindling fleet of MQ-9A Reapers. The force is seeking a unit price of around USD 10 million for the Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV), which is considerably less than the USD 30-50 million dollars for a fully equipped aircraft. The urgency to bring in the new aircraft is caused by the loss of many of these aircraft in the ongoing operations in Iran as well as over Yemen.
The new drone programme, called the Massed Modular Aircraft (MMA), is expected to retain the MQ-9A's ISR and strike capability according to Air Force Lieutenant General Christopher Niemi, the service's Chief Modernization Officer. Programme requirements call for a speed of at least 200 knots, a payload capacity of 2,800 pounds, an unrefuelled combat radius of 2,300 nautical miles (4,200 km), a ferry range of up to 8,000 nautical miles (14,000 km) and the ability to operate from runways as short as 6,000 feet. The MMA is expected to be built around a modular, open-architecture design that makes future upgrades easier.
IRGC Claims US MQ-9 Reaper Drone Shot Down Over Strait Of Hormuz Amid Iran-US Escalation
General Atomics, the original maker of the Reaper, has already responded with its Wildfire drone, pitched as delivering everything that made the Reaper effective, only sooner and at a fraction of the cost. With combat losses mounting and the Pentagon keen to field something more expendable and affordable at scale, the MMA programme looks set to reshape how America's next generation of drones gets built.
The US military has lost at least 45 MQ-9 Reaper drones during its ongoing conflict with Iran, close to a quarter of the roughly 185-strong fleet it started with, split between 165 with the Air Force and 20 with the Marine Corps. Operating heavily around the Strait of Hormuz, the drones have proven easy targets for Iran and its regional proxies given their slow speed and low-altitude profile, with some losses also traced to communication link failures rather than enemy fire.
For nearly two decades, the Reaper has been the quiet workhorse of America's Central Command operations, flying surveillance and strike missions across Iraq, Afghanistan, Yemen and Syria in largely uncontested skies. That flight profile, slow and predictable, worked brilliantly against terror organisations without an effective air defence capability. Against Iran, the same characteristics have turned into a liability, making it a comparatively easy kill.
India, too, is buying into this same platform across all three services, eight each for the Army and Air Force and 15 for the Navy, in a deal worth over USD 3 billion, drawn largely by its 40-hour endurance and the surveillance picture that offers over the Indian Ocean and along India's land borders. Induction is expected by 2029, with 21 of the drones to be assembled domestically and 34 per cent local component sourcing. The Navy, which already leases two Reapers, has just signed a fresh Rs 1,943 crore deal to extend that lease by 30 months, underlining just how central this aircraft has become to India's own surveillance plans, contested skies notwithstanding.

deep-tech-a11c961a29.headline: Quantum Foundry Copenhagen Plans 5,300-Square-Meter Chip Facility
deep-tech-a11c961a29.fulltext:
Insider Brief
- Quantum Foundry Copenhagen plans to open a 5,300-square-meter quantum chip fabrication facility in Copenhagen in 2027 to support commercial-scale manufacturing.
- The facility will combine nanofabrication, characterization, testing, chip assembly, packaging and ultra-high-vacuum manufacturing capabilities.
- The Novo Nordisk Foundation has committed more than DKK 2.9 billion (€390 million) to quantum technologies, including a program targeting a fault-tolerant quantum computer before 2034.
PRESS RELEASE — Today, Quantum Foundry Copenhagen and the Novo Nordisk Foundation announce plans to establish a new 5,300 m² quantum chip fabrication facility in Copenhagen. The facility will develop and scale the advanced manufacturing equipment needed to produce the next generation of quantum chips and strengthen Europe’s position in an increasingly competitive global quantum landscape.
While Europe has built one of the world’s strongest research environments in quantum science, global leadership in quantum technologies will ultimately depend not only on scientific breakthroughs, but also on the ability to turn these breakthroughs into commercial products at scale. The fabrication of high-quality quantum chips, the specialised core processing units inside a quantum computer, is a crucial part of that process.
Quantum technologies have the potential to solve problems that are beyond the reach of today’s most powerful computers. In the future, they could help researchers develop new medicines faster, design more sustainable materials, optimise energy systems, and strengthen cybersecurity.
Owned by the Novo Nordisk Foundation, Quantum Foundry Copenhagen is a specialised technology company developing proprietary tools, materials and processes for quantum chip manufacturing. The company’s new facility will uniquely combine laboratory space for nanofabrication of quantum materials, advanced characterisation, testing, chip assembly and packaging with ultra-high vacuum manufacturing capabilities and through this offer wafer fabrication for quantum technology vendors globally on commercial terms.
“Our vision is to become a world-leading quantum chip manufacturer, supplying Europe with advanced, next-generation quantum computing processors and enabling quantum companies to scale production. We aim to build state-of-the-art quantum production lines and support a sustainable deep-tech industry that can help shape the future of quantum technology,” says Peter Krogstrup, CEO, Quantum Foundry Copenhagen.
Quantum Foundry Copenhagen is built on the Novo Nordisk Foundation’s long-term commitment to quantum technologies. The Foundation has committed more than DKK 2.9 billion (EUR 390 million) to the field, including the Novo Nordisk Foundation Quantum Computing Programme at the Niels Bohr Institute, University of Copenhagen. The aim of the Programme is to develop Denmark’s first fully functional fault-tolerant quantum computer before 2034. The new chip facility will collaborate closely with the Foundation’s quantum programme, creating a unique link between frontier research, talent development and industrial manufacturing capabilities.
“At the Novo Nordisk Foundation, we believe quantum technologies will be one of the most defining scientific and technological fields of this century. That is why we have made a significant long-term commitment to building a world-class quantum ecosystem in Denmark and Europe. Quantum Foundry Copenhagen is an important part of that ambition, helping connect investments in research with the industrial capabilities needed to support Europe’s ability to transform quantum breakthroughs into technologies that can benefit society, strengthen competitiveness and address some of the world’s most complex challenges,” says Professor Mads Krogsgaard Thomsen, CEO of the Novo Nordisk Foundation.
Both Denmark and the European Union are currently intensifying efforts to strengthen quantum innovation and industrial capacity. Through the Quantum Europe Strategy, the forthcoming Quantum Act, and a growing focus on technological sovereignty, the European Union is prioritising the commercialisation, manufacturing and deployment of quantum technologies.
At the same time, Denmark’s forthcoming quantum strategy From quantum research to quantum industry reflects this same transition, positioning Denmark to play a leading role in uniting Europe’s capabilities into a resilient, scalable and globally competitive industrial platform.
“Quantum technologies are expected to become a foundational technology platform for the future, much like semiconductors, computing and the internet have been in previous generations. If Europe is to succeed in quantum, it must not repeat the pattern from earlier technology waves, where fundamental science was strong in Europe but industrial scale-up, platforms and global champions emerged elsewhere. Developing this capacity marks an important step towards positioning Europe centrally in the global quantum ecosystem and building resilience,” says Lene Oddershede, Chief Scientific Officer, Novo Nordisk Foundation.
The new facility is expected to open in 2027.

climate-energy-406df38c83.headline: Beyond record-low tariffs: Fixing India’s renewable energy auction model
climate-energy-406df38c83.fulltext:
- Renewable

Beyond record-low tariffs: Fixing India’s renewable energy auction model
The energy crisis is a wake-up call for India to strategize the much sought after long-term energy independence of the country. The twin targets of Vikshit Bharat and energy independence by 2047 have become the guiding policy directives. However, the complexities arise in the form of operational hurdles encountered in transforming these goals into implementable actions.
In its pursuit to become an energy independent country, renewable energy has received dominant policy attention, emerging as the key future alternative option among all possible options for the country. So far, most of the renewable energy additions are supplementing the current energy systems by serving part of the increased energy demand, rather than replacing the incumbent fossil heavy energy system.
However, ambitions run high to scale up the renewable energy to serve as the mainstay energy system of the country sooner than later. There has been a dramatic surge in the renewable energy deployment capacity touching the record high of 275 GW by April 2026.This clearly manifests the bold commitment to translate the renewable energy policies into actions in driving the country towards the trajectory of energy security and sustainability.
Auctions as dominant energy procurement mechanism
Auctions, more precisely known as ‘e-reverse auctions’ have emerged as the dominant procurement strategic pathway in driving the renewable energy growth in India. While policy thrusts for acceleration of renewable energy growth in the country have historically been focused on publicly supported incentive schemes such as Accelerated Depreciation (AD), Generation Based Incentives (GBI), Feed-in-Tariff (FiT), Viability Gap Funding (VGF), recent emphasis is more on market led instruments like auctions.
In fact, auctions have emerged as the primary vehicle and have evolved as the key institutional architecture for the renewable energy procurement in the country. Procurement through auctions is conducted through standardised reverse bidding mechanism. Solar Energy Corporation of India (SECI), as the pivotal institutional entity, governs the auction mechanism by issuing a Request for Selection (RfS) detailing necessary bidding requirements such as total capacity on offer, technology type, project location, bid validity etc.
Developers bidding the lowest tariff per kilowatt hour (kWh) win the bid, and the capacity allocation continues until tendered quantity gets exhausted. SECI has so far carried out at least 19 wind tranches, 18 ISTS (Inter-State Transmission System) solar auctions, along with 8 hybrid wind-solar tranches.
The tariff race leading to winners’ curse
The reverse auction mechanism is built on the philosophy that the competitive spirit could drive down the price of renewable energy, which would eventually generate larger economic as well as the social benefits. However, in case of energy auctions the developers bidding for low price is premised on the assumptions of falling technology costs, cheap land availability for deployment, possible quick grid access, and smooth completion of the project.
In reality project implementations often face several operational hurdles leading to a situation called ‘Winners’ Curse’. Winner’s curse refers to a state where the developers win the project through low-cost bidding yet face herculean tasks of arranging the necessary infrastructure support systems such as acquisition of land, getting the right of ways (RoW) clearance, availing the transmission lines, and resolving grid connectivity issues in operationalising the project.
Often the breakneck competition at the bidding level drives the winning tariff to a point where project commissioning and project operation appear financially not viable. Besides, the auction regime has led to the emergence of a new class of large-scale independent power producers (IPPs), big renewable energy developers and business concentration. Some studies have shown that the top ten developers account for 36 per cent of India’s operational renewable energy capacity and this share is projected to rise to close to 60 per cent by 2030.
The way forward
India’s auction regime has clearly delivered record-low tariffs, built project pipelines, strengthened the developer ecosystem, and laid the foundation to achieve the larger goals of achieving net zero emission by 2070, but is riddled with a number of systemic anomalies calling for strategic policy attention.
- Going beyond capacity chasing, it is crucial that mechanisms be developed to translate the contracted capacity to effective power purchase agreements. This clearly reflects the need for closed loop monitoring and execution of auctions as practised in countries like South Africa, where bidding requires information on site name, grid availability integral part of pre-qualification.
− The auction design must evolve from a low-cost discovery approach to building a system.
The bidding needs to be examined holistically, including land readiness, transmission connectivity, ecological clearance, and not merely on financial stringency.
− The cancelled tenders should be considered as potential option for improvement, through the examination of the root cause for cancellation and low realisation rates.
− Finally, the demand and supply imbalance could be mitigated through institutional
capacity building. Otherwise, the growing ambition and pipeline of projects may remain limited to paperwork.
India has the structure, the mechanism and the ambition in place. The need is to streamline the auctions to deliver the desired outcomes. The idea of energy beyond a threshold level, is no longer an energy problem alone, rather a systemic issue requiring an ‘Energy+’ approach.

climate-energy-cc8575d3c3.headline: India drafts mandatory battery storage rules for new renewable energy projects
climate-energy-cc8575d3c3.fulltext:
NEW DELHI: India is considering mandatory battery storage for new solar and onshore wind projects from July 2027 to improve the ability of the power grid to store and dispatch renewable electricity when required, Reuters reported.
Under draft regulations prepared by the Central Electricity Authority (CEA), all new solar and onshore wind projects commissioned from July 1, 2027, would be required to install battery storage equivalent to at least 10% of their generating capacity, with a minimum storage duration of two hours.
The requirement would become more stringent from July 2029. Projects commissioned after July 1, 2029, would need to provide at least four hours of storage while retaining the 10% capacity requirement.
The proposal comes as India rapidly expands its renewable energy capacity and faces increasing challenges in managing fluctuations in solar and wind generation. Battery energy storage systems can absorb excess electricity generated during periods of high renewable output and release it when demand rises, helping reduce renewable power curtailment.
India, the world’s third-largest solar power generator, curtailed nearly 14% of its solar generation between April and June amid surplus daytime electricity and constraints in transmission infrastructure.
The proposed rules also seek to make grid-forming inverter capabilities mandatory for clean energy projects commissioned after July 2027.
Grid-forming inverters can help maintain grid voltage and frequency stability without relying entirely on conventional generation sources. Their importance is expected to increase as the share of solar and wind power in India’s electricity mix continues to rise.
The proposed storage and grid-support requirements are aimed at improving the reliability of renewable power while enabling greater integration of variable solar and wind generation into the national grid.

climate-energy-c4476f978d.headline: Faster EV Adoption and India’s Import Bill
climate-energy-c4476f978d.fulltext:
Context: A new International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT) study estimates that faster electric vehicle adoption, combined with domestic battery manufacturing, could reduce India’s annual oil and battery import bill by up to $125 billion by 2050.
About Faster EV Adoption and India’s Import Bill:
What It Is?
- The ICCT study assesses how different levels of EV adoption and domestic battery-cell manufacturing could affect India’s oil and battery import payments between 2024 and 2050.
- It evaluates three EV pathways—Baseline, Momentum and Ambitious—along with different levels of battery manufacturing localisation.
Aim: To assess whether rapid transport electrification and battery localisation can reduce India’s dependence on imported petroleum and batteries while strengthening energy security and domestic manufacturing.
Key Findings:
- $125 Billion Potential Savings: Ambitious EV adoption with high battery localisation could reduce the annual import bill from $153 billion to about $28 billion by 2050.
- EV Adoption is the Main Driver: Faster electrification alone could save around $94 billion annually, even if India continues importing all battery cells.
- Localisation Adds Savings: High domestic battery manufacturing could provide an additional $31 billion in annual savings by 2050.
- Battery Demand to Surge: EV battery demand could reach around 573 GWh annually by 2050 under faster electrification scenarios, making domestic cell manufacturing strategically important.
- Protection from Oil Shocks: Higher global crude prices substantially increase the benefits of electrification by reducing India’s exposure to volatile petroleum import costs.
Significance:
- Reduces dependence on imported crude oil and vulnerability to geopolitical and global oil-price shocks.
- Battery localisation can strengthen Atmanirbhar Bharat, domestic value chains, technology capabilities and EV manufacturing.
- Faster electrification can lower transport-sector fossil-fuel consumption and support India’s decarbonisation and net-zero transition.

Ford India plans mega EV facility in Chennai, eyes Asia-Pacific hub for affordable EVs
ADVERTISEMENT
Ford Motor Company is looking to develop its Maraimalai Nagar facility near Chennai into a major electric-vehicle manufacturing hub, with plans for a brownfield expansion that could combine EV assembly with the manufacture of batteries, cells, electric motors and other critical components, according to sources familiar with the development.
It has also been learnt from well-informed sources that the proposed facility is also being positioned as an Asia-Pacific hub for affordable electric vehicles, with production expected to cater primarily to export markets. The plan could significantly expand Ford’s manufacturing footprint in India and provide the company with an integrated base to develop and produce lower-cost EVs for the region.
“Ford is looking at Chennai not just as a powertrain manufacturing base but as a larger EV manufacturing hub for the Asia-Pacific region. The focus is expected to be on affordable electric vehicles, with the facility potentially serving both the regional and global export markets,” a person familiar with the development said.
Ford, however, has not publicly confirmed an EV manufacturing programme at the Chennai facility. A Ford India spokesperson, when contacted by Fortune India, stated, “There is no change to what we announced last year. Our Chennai facility will manufacture powertrains for export only. We have not provided details of the type of powertrain or export markets at this point.”
It may be recalled that Ford had in October 2025 announced an investment of ₹3,250 crore to revive manufacturing operations at Maraimalai Nagar. The programme is focused on powertrains for export markets and is expected to have annual production capacity of around 2.35 lakh units.
Brownfield expansion could create integrated EV base
The proposed expansion would repurpose and expand Ford’s existing Chennai facility rather than involve a new greenfield plant. Besides EV assembly, the manufacturing ecosystem could include battery packs, battery cells, electric motors and other electric powertrain components, allowing Ford to localise a larger portion of the EV value chain and potentially improve cost competitiveness.
Industry estimates put the potential investment for an integrated EV and battery manufacturing operation at ₹15,000-20,000 crore, although Ford has not disclosed any investment figure for such a programme.
The scale would be comparable with some of the larger EV and battery projects under development in India. Tata Group’s Agratas is setting up a 20 GWh battery-cell manufacturing facility in Sanand, Gujarat, with an initial investment of ₹13,000 crore. VinFast has committed an initial $500 million investment to its Tamil Nadu manufacturing facility, with an option to increase its overall India investment to as much as $2 billion.
Affordable EVs could drive next phase
The potential project comes as India’s EV market expands rapidly. India recorded 15.41 lakh EV registrations in the first half of 2026, up 43% year-on-year, while EV penetration rose to 11.43% from 8% a year earlier, according to JMK Research, citing Vahan data.
Electric passenger-vehicle registrations grew 83% year-on-year in H1 2026, according to JMK Research, as automakers expanded their EV portfolios across price points.
Puneet Gupta, Director, India & ASEAN Automotive Market at S&P Global Mobility, said the next phase of EV adoption would depend on automakers making electric vehicles available at more accessible price points, along with greater localisation, broader product portfolios and improving charging infrastructure.
“For Ford, a potential EV manufacturing programme in Chennai could provide an opportunity to rebuild its manufacturing footprint in India while leveraging the country’s engineering and supplier ecosystem to develop and produce more affordable electric vehicles for the wider Asia-Pacific market,” he added.
Chennai’s second innings
It may be recalled that Ford stopped domestic vehicle production in India in 2021 after years of losses and low capacity utilisation, but retained its Chennai facility and subsequently decided to revive manufacturing operations.
Its return has so far centred on powertrain manufacturing for export markets. A potential EV programme could broaden that strategy by transforming the plant into an integrated electric-vehicle manufacturing base.
If realised, the project could give Ford a larger role in India’s EV ecosystem while establishing the country as a regional manufacturing base for affordable electric mobility.
