agritech-90eadac678.headline: Explained: Why a Warm Winter and Monsoon Deficit Could Trigger India’s Next Big Food Price Shock
agritech-90eadac678.fulltext:
Explained: Why a Warm Winter and Monsoon Deficit Could Trigger India’s Next Big Food Price Shock
Summarized by AI; it may make mistakes. Check important info
India’s widening monsoon deficit and volatile weather patterns threaten to spark a fresh surge in food inflation, with the India Meteorological Department (IMD) warning that 350 out of 741 monitored districts (47%) face severe rainfall shortfalls. The economic risk builds as severe regional drought damages standing summer Kharif crops and endangers the upcoming winter Rabi sowing cycle.
While headline figures show an overall national rainfall deficit of roughly 14%, single-digit and low-double-digit national averages mask deep localized drought across primary farming belts. With the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) confirming that a "very strong" El Niño will persist with near 100% certainty through February 2027, policymakers face a multi-quarter inflationary challenge spanning food staples, edible oils, and pulses.
National Averages Mask Ground-Level Drought Pressure
The nationwide 14% deficit hides an extraordinarily uneven distribution of rainfall. Heavily localized downpours in select pockets have skewed national totals upward, obscuring severe soil moisture depletion across primary agricultural states like Bihar, East Uttar Pradesh, Jharkhand, Gangetic West Bengal, interior Karnataka, and Rayalaseema.
August registered a national mean temperature of 28.01°C—the highest August baseline since 1901. Intense heat combined with deficient rainfall drove up evaporation rates, shrinking reservoir levels across major river basins to three-year lows. The rapid depletion of surface water reserves removes a critical buffer against rising food production costs and groundwater pumping expenses.
Damaged Kharif Output Drives Up Immediate Food Prices
Deficient moisture during critical growth stages has directly reduced Kharif crop coverage and yields, feeding straight into immediate retail price risks:
• Paddy / Rice: Rainfed belts face delayed flowering and stunted growth. Rice acreage dropped significantly across key eastern states, creating immediate supply pressure on the primary domestic staple.
• Pulses & Oilseeds: Tur, Urad, and Soybean experienced notable acreage declines as dry topsoil delayed planting, raising import dependency and domestic retail costs.
• Coarse Cereals: Rainfed Maize and Bajra crops suffered severe moisture stress during early vegetative phases, threatening animal feed stocks and industrial supply chains.
WMO Forecast: Prolonged Warmth Threatens Rabi Crop Yields
The inflationary shock will extend well beyond summer harvests into the upcoming winter Rabi season. The WMO confirms that persistent Pacific warming will split weather risks across the country through early 2027:
• South India (Northeast Monsoon): Unusually volatile, high-intensity rain events over hard, parched ground risk flash flooding rather than providing steady, usable irrigation.
• North India (Winter Season): El Niño will disrupt traditional cold wave patterns across the Indo-Gangetic Plains. Although Western Disturbances will bring sporadic winter rain, significantly elevated day and night temperatures will eliminate the winter chill needed for proper crop development.
Winter Staples Face Severe Heat Stress
An unseasonably warm winter directly threatens key cold-weather crops, escalating food price volatility well into mid-2027:
• Wheat: Hyper-sensitive to thermal shifts, wheat faces elevated night temperatures during critical flowering in February. Terminal heat stress causes premature grain shrivelling and yield cuts, directly threatening retail market supply.
• Mustard & Rapeseed: High October–November temperatures lower seed oil content and increase crop exposure to early aphid infestations, risking higher edible oil inflation.
• Chickpea (Gram): Sown on residual moisture, chickpea acreage will shrink unless farmers rely on expensive groundwater pumping, pushing up farm-gate costs.
With nearly half of India's districts dry and reservoir reserves severely depleted, consecutive crop disruptions threaten to push consumer food inflation higher over the next two agricultural cycles.

agritech-fbd2d97556.headline: From Himalayas to Deccan: How droughts and glacial melt reshape India's water reservoirs
agritech-fbd2d97556.fulltext:
Climate Change
From Himalayas to Deccan: How droughts and glacial melt reshape India's water reservoirs 
Extreme droughts are reshaping India’s waterscapes: small lakes dry up quickest, large reservoirs lose volume, and mountain glaciers rewrite the story. Read the findings of this important study to know more.
Surface water bodies (SWBs) such as lakes, ponds, and reservoirs are valuable freshwater resources providing water for drinking, agriculture, and industrial use while supporting biodiversity and aquatic ecosystems and maintaining the ecological sustainability of the surrounding environment. They also play a crucial role in the hydrological cycle by acting as buffers, regulating surface runoff, and aiding in storage and distribution of water.
India has a vast number of SWBs distributed across different climatic zones. They are categorised into small (0.1–1 km2), medium (1–10 km2), and large (>10 km2) and are becoming increasingly vulnerable to climate extremes, particularly droughts, disrupting the balance between inflows and outflows. However, very little information is available on the impact of droughts on SWBs in India.
This open access study titled ‘Drought-driven shrinkage of surface water bodies in India ‘ by M Niranjannaik and Vimal Mishra, published in iScience aims at exploring the impacts of droughts and their severity on shrinkage patterns of SWBs across different climatic zones in India. The study examines Lansat satellite-derived area data on 10,476 SWBs during 1990–2017 to understand their shrinkage patterns.
The climate zones examined in the study include:
- The Tropical wet zone, or the tropical monsoon/humid climate zone that includes the Western Coastal Plains & Western Ghats, the Northeastern States and the island territories of Lakshadweep and Andaman and Nicobar islands.
- The tropical wet and dry regions include Central India, mainly inland areas of Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, and Chhattisgarh; Eastern States such as parts of Odisha, West Bengal, and southern Assam; and the Southern Interior, which includes the majority of the interior Deccan Plateau, excluding the coastal strips and the rain-shadow semi-arid zones
- Arid zones include major parts of Rajasthan, Gujarat, southern parts of Punjab and Haryana and a small portion of the Deccan Peninsula in the states of Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Maharashtra
- Semiarid zones include the states of Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu
- Humid subtropical zones include parts of northern and eastern India, including the Gangetic plains
- Mountain frost: Trans Himalayas and the cold deserts.
The spatial distribution of surface water bodies in India
A preliminary look at the shrinking patterns indicates that nearly half (44.5%) of the SWBs have shrunk in area, while 29.4% of the SWBs show a significant increase in surface area. The long-term trends show a pronounced decline in several subbasins across the north and south Indian regions. Approximately 80% of SWBs in the Ghaggar subbasin within the semi-arid zone exhibit a significant decreasing trend. Widespread declines are also seen in the Ganga Basin, where 60%–80% of SWBs show significant reductions in the Gandak, Sone, upper Gomti, and upper Yamuna subbasins under a humid subtropical climate. Additionally, 40%–60% of SWBs in the Krishna, Pennar, and Kaveri subbasins of the semi-arid zone display significant decreasing trends.
In contrast, more than 80% of SWBs in the Mountain Frost climate zone exhibit a significantly increasing trend due to glacial melting as a result of rising temperatures. More than 40% of SWBs in the westward-flowing lower Narmada and Bhadar subbasins show an increasing trend. Moderate increase (40%–60%) in surface area in SWBs is seen in the west-flowing river subbasins such as the Narmada, Sabarmati, Mahi, Luni, and Shetranjali, as well as the east-flowing lower Godavari sub-basin, which is predominantly located in semi-arid climate zones. These increases can be attributed to an increase in rainfall over the region.
What happens during dry and wet years
During wet years, the majority of SWBs (80%) show an expansion of water area, with SWBs in the tropical wet and dry and semi-arid climate zones showing pronounced water gain during wet years. In contrast, 67% of SWBs in the Mountain Frost climate zone show shrinkage in water area by around 15.7 km2 despite an increase in rainfall. This could be due to a decline in mean annual temperature that freezes the SWBs, causing shrinkage in the surface area in the Mountain Frost region.
During dry years, most SWBs (82%) show shrinkage in surface area across all climate zones, except for the Mountain Frost climate zone, where the majority of SWBs show expansion. The SWBs in semi-arid climate zones experience the most pronounced shrinkage (20%), reflecting their strong dependence on rainfall. In contrast, the expansion of SWB in the Mountain Frost climate zone is due to warmer temperatures, which melt the glaciers and snow, resulting in an increase in water availability.
Also read:Himalayan lakes, under stress!
Summer monsoon
The summer-monsoon season is the most important source and a critical period that helps in filling up surface water bodies, thus expanding their surface area. During the dry summer monsoons, the majority of the SWBs in the semi-arid, humid subtropical, and tropical wet and dry climate zones of central India exhibit high shrinkage (>10%). However, SWBs in the Mountain Frost and Arid climate zones are the least affected. A dry monsoon alone causes a 5% decline in the mean SWB area in India. Winter droughts lead to a 2.5% shrinkage in the semi-arid and tropical wet and dry climate zones of the central Indian region.
Dry summers and winters
Successive dry seasons within a single water year result in the highest water loss. The SWBs experiencing consecutive dry summer-monsoon and winter seasons of the water cycle show an 8.5% water area shrinkage – nearly three times greater shrinkage than that affected by a single summer-monsoon dry season.
Dry winters and premonsoon
Dry winter and pre-monsoon seasons lead to a decline of 2.7% and 0.65%, respectively.
The dry monsoon season has the greatest impact, even when other seasons are wet, resulting in a 1.33% reduction in surface area. During dry seasons and years, the highest shrinkage in surface water area is observed in the semi-arid, humid subtropical, and tropical wet and dry climate zones driven by high water demand, limited winter rainfall, and rapid depletion of surface water reserves. In contrast, the SWBs in the Mountain Frost climate zone show an expansion of water area driven by snowmelt due to warming.
The impact of drought is most evident during the summer-monsoon and winter seasons, and successive dry conditions in these seasons increase water loss by three times compared to individual seasons.
As droughts get worse, larger lakes and reservoirs shrink more than smaller ones, except in the Mountain Frost zones, where the SWB area is found to expand as drought severity increases.
Arid & semi-arid SWBs are the most vulnerable, where medium and large SWBs lose >13% area under extreme drought. In tropical wet & humid subtropical zones, all sizes shrink, with large SWBs losing up to 10%, as high population and farming make the stress worse. In tropical wet & dry zones, large, shallow SWBs decline sharply because they depend on rainfall. With Mountain Frost in the Himalayas, small SWBs expand during moderate drought due to glacier melt. But under severe drought, medium and large SWBs also shrink.
Thus, small SWBs are more resilient and withstand the impacts of severe droughts, except in glacier-fed zones where they can even expand. In contrast, large SWBs are the most exposed and suffer the biggest losses in surface area. Arid/semi-arid zones are the hardest hit overall.
The spatial distribution of SWBs by shrinkage rate.
Small SWBs show the highest shrinkage rate due to limited storage and fast response to drought, while medium SWBs show moderate shrinkage. Large SWBs show the lowest shrinkage rates. Thus, small SWBs shrink the fastest in all the zones. However, mountain frost zones (Himalayas) show a different behaviour, with small SWBs showing less shrinkage than medium/large ones, and sometimes even expanding during dry years due to glacier and snowmelt.
The impact of increasing drought intensity on the SWB area accelerates shrinkage among all SWB sizes in India. However, large SWBs exhibit the highest decline in water area as the drought severity increases, likely due to a decline in runoff and an increase in evaporation. In contrast, small SWBs shrink faster relative to their size, which might be due to shallow depth and limited inflow, making them more vulnerable to short-term climate stress.
The spatial variability in the SWB area is also affected by land-use and cover (LULC) changes and regional climatic contrasts. For example, in the Ganga plains, cropland expansion combined with declining rainfall and rising temperatures has resulted in a substantial reduction of the SWB area exceeding 60%. In addition, intensive groundwater extraction for irrigation has significantly depleted groundwater storage in the region. Similarly, SWBs in the South Indian sub-basins (Godavari, Krishna, Cauvery, and Penna) have also experienced major declines (40%–60%), despite increasing precipitation and relatively stable temperatures due to cropland expansion, increasing impervious surfaces, and unsustainable water management. In contrast, in the Mountain Frost climate zones, more than 80% of the SWBs show an increasing trend, primarily influenced by glacier and snow cover loss. The snow cover loss is driven by a significant increase in temperature and declining rainfall.
More than 40% of SWBs in the western-flowing (i.e., Narmada, Mahi, and Sabarmati) and eastern-flowing Mahanadi Basins show a significant increasing trend, despite rising temperatures, driven by increased rainfall. Declining water areas are closely associated with increasing temperatures and reduced rainfall, and excessive use of surface water and groundwater extraction for irrigation during drought periods further exacerbates long-term stress on SWBs.
Addressing the water area changes, shrinkage rate, and shrinkage duration under increasing drought intensities can provide valuable information on the vulnerability of SWBs and help in developing drought preparedness and water scarcity mitigation strategies, enabling policymakers and local stakeholders to implement actions on time. The high sensitivity of SWBs to droughts, particularly in arid, semi-arid, humid subtropical, and tropical wet and dry regions, has important implications for water policy and drought management.
The results show that:
- The drought impact on small, medium, and large SWBs reveals that small SWBs require more attention due to their rapid depletion, while large SWBs need basin-scale coordination to reduce the losses during prolonged droughts.
- Groundwater governance plays a crucial role in maintaining SWBs, as excessive pumping can transform SWBs from recharge zones into groundwater sinks and vice versa, worsening the impacts of droughts. Integrated surface- and groundwater management policies are therefore essential for sustaining both surface and subsurface water resources during droughts.
- Protecting SWBs from encroachment is important to preserve natural drainage pathways, and restricting land-use change within optimal catchment buffer zones improves rainfall capture, slows down water loss during droughts, and sustains storage. In river-connected systems, maintaining minimum environmental flows can further prolong downstream SWB persistence during droughts.

agritech-e1e1a43ef5.headline: Climate Crisis and Farm Distress Push Indian Farmers Out
agritech-e1e1a43ef5.fulltext:
In some ways, Jiyalal, once a farmer dependent on the vagaries of the monsoon, is a much-relieved man. Hailing from Mahua village in Uttar Pradesh, he has left his fields behind for the city. “A land that gives home but no food is worse than one that gives food but no home,” he says.
After leaving home, Jiyalal migrated to the national capital with little in his pocket and the hope of finding work that could meet his family’s needs, something he could no longer manage through farming. After years of toiling in his fields, he now works as a daily-wage labourer at different construction sites, earning about Rs.800 a day. He makes around Rs.20,000 a month, considerably more than what he could earn from farming.
Jiyalal’s case is not unique. Farmers across the country are increasingly leaving their farms as uncertainty, inadequate government support, and erratic weather conditions pull them away from their roots and push them towards other professions in bigger cities such as Delhi. It is not necessarily what they want to do, but it is what they are forced to do when everything else fails.
For Jiyalal, the uncertainty of agriculture eventually outweighed the comfort of home. “Sometimes it rains, sometimes it doesn’t. There is no certainty. I left home so my family could eat,” he says.
The trend is not new and has persisted for decades. A 2014 report of a survey conducted by the Centre for the Study of Developing Societies (CSDS), an autonomous research institute in Delhi for the social sciences and humanities, found that 76 per cent of farmers would prefer to take up non-farming work. Of these, 61 per cent said they would rather be employed in cities for better access to education, healthcare, and stable employment. Meanwhile, 70 per cent of respondents said their crops had been damaged by unseasonal rains, droughts, floods, or pest attacks, with such losses pushing many farmers off their land.
Across India, thousands of farmers, like 56-year-old Mohammad Naushad, share Jiyalal’s plight, as they have been forced to leave their ancestral fields by erratic weather, inadequate state support, and stagnant prices.
For such farmers, farming has become a trade of loss. Naushad, who left his family behind, once farmed in Bihar’s Katihar district until he could no longer sustain himself through farming. Now he works as a scrap dealer in Delhi. He recalls: “The seeds cost more than the money we made from selling our crops. The government never looked into the matter, and if there was any policy, it never reached us.”
His experience comes against a larger economic imbalance in Indian agriculture. The Economic Survey 2025-26 says agriculture and allied activities account for 46.1 per cent of India’s workforce but contribute only about one-fifth of national income. It identifies fragmented landholdings, limited irrigation and access to quality inputs, low mechanisation, and stagnating yields in several crops and regions as continuing constraints on productivity and farmer incomes.
Slow growth
A PRS Legislative Research analysis of the 2026-27 Demand for Grants for Agriculture and Farmers Welfare similarly says agriculture and allied activities employ about 46 per cent of India’s workforce but account for 18 per cent of Gross Value Added. Between 2011-12 and 2024-25, the sector grew at an average annual rate of 4 per cent, compared with the 6 per cent overall GDP growth. Within agriculture, crop output grew at about 2 per cent annually between 2011-12 and 2023-24, compared with the 5 per cent growth in allied activities such as livestock, forestry, and fisheries.
Sanjay Mehta, an expert on migrant issues and a migrant workers’ rights activist from Jharkhand, said: “Uncertainty is the main reason why farmers are migrating and abandoning farming. It has become insufficient to meet the needs of the people employed in the sector. The cash flow is hand to mouth, with nothing more to spend.” Mehta contested the 2024 Lok Sabha election but did not win.
The crisis facing India’s farmlands is deepened by climate change, which has turned what were once predictable seasons into cycles of floods and droughts and worsened the conditions faced by farmers like Purab, a 26-year-old farmer from Katera town in Jhansi, Uttar Pradesh.
He abandoned his 10-acre farm after unpredictable weather conditions repeatedly spoiled his crops, ultimately forcing him to give up his generational work on the farm and take up work at a construction site in Delhi’s Shaheen Bagh.
“At times there would be too much rain, and at times not at all,” he says, describing how erratic weather has shattered his livelihood. “We never received any support from the government. Now there’s a whole group of us here, farmers-turned-construction workers.” Purab pointed to a large group of construction workers, all of whom had left their families and farms.
He toiled on a 10-acre farm that sits right at the upper bound of the medium farmer category, just shy of official “large farmer” status, which requires 10 hectares (~24.7 acres), as classified by the structure defined by the Union Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare. “Migration is not just restricted to small farmers, but it extends to farmers who hold bigger lands,” says Mehta.
The experience is consistent with findings from the Development Intelligence Unit (DIU), a data-driven initiative focussed on providing analytics for development, and the Forum of Enterprises for Equitable Development. A survey of 6,615 marginal farmers across 21 States found that 83 per cent of marginal farmers in villages affected by severe weather conditions had changed their livelihood pattern, compared with 61 per cent in villages that had not experienced such conditions. The survey also found that 80 per cent of marginal farmers had suffered crop losses due to adverse climatic events over the previous five years.
The Economic Survey 2025-26 also identifies climate variability, erratic rainfall, and extreme weather events as direct risks to crop yields and farm incomes. It notes that continued dependence on rainfall and inadequate irrigation leave farmers vulnerable to climate shocks.
PRS identifies the same structural vulnerability, pointing to dependence on rain-fed agriculture and rising water stress as major challenges. It notes that irrigation remains uneven across crops and regions.
The weather is not the only reason farmers want out. Another report titled State of Marginal Farmers of India, published by the DIU highlights the concern. It found that 83 per cent of farmers in villages affected by adverse climatic events were forced to change their livelihood, compared with 61 per cent in unaffected areas, a stark indication of how deeply the climate crisis is reshaping rural India.
For Girija Shankar, a farmer-turned-fruit vendor from Bihar, migration is the only way to survive. “Farming couldn’t do enough to feed our family,” he says. “Here, at least I can earn and send money back home,” Shankar adds.
His wife still cultivates their small field, but the household now depends heavily on his earnings in Delhi. Ironically, Shankar uses his city income to modernise his family’s farm. Yet when asked if he would ever return, he said he wouldn’t: “There are better earnings in the city.”
Women’s unpaid work
The migration pattern in the stories of Shankar and Jiyalal brings out a bigger challenge that women farmers face. They work in fields, but their efforts are often not recognised or rewarded, and they receive no monetary value for their work. Jiyalal earns cash in Delhi while his wife continues working on the farm, with the produce helping sustain the household.
“Back in Mahua, my wife still works as a farmer on a small patch of land to supplement the family’s food supply. The money I earn here now could be used for other things and to meet the food needs of the family. My wife works on our farm. It’s only enough to feed us food, but not enough to bring us any money,” Jiyalal said.
The women’s work reflects a wider, often invisible, part of India’s agricultural economy. A 2026 report by grain commerce platform Arya.ag, “Her Harvest 2026: The Hidden Cost of Women’s Invisible Work in Indian Agriculture”, found that 50.5 per cent of women working in agriculture are recorded as unpaid helpers on family farms, compared with 21.7 per cent of men.
Down To Earth, reporting on the study, said women make up about 48 per cent of India’s agricultural workforce but hold only 13.96 per cent of operational holdings.
The report says women who are not formally recognised as cultivators can face restricted access to credit, agricultural inputs, procurement systems, and government schemes. It estimates that this gap between women’s agricultural labour and their formal recognition could be associated with annual agricultural output losses of Rs.1.2 lakh crore to Rs.2 lakh crore.
“Women farmers don’t receive proper training to use the updated technology. They largely work as secondary workers who barely receive any monetary credit for it,” says Mehta. He adds: “In the last five years, the migration pattern has increased. There are more than an estimated 20,000 farmers who have migrated.”
The cities where most of the farmers go are Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, and Hyderabad. The pattern is not just restricted to India but transcends borders, as countries like Saudi Arabia and other African countries also become a destination for these migrant farmers.
But migration does not solve their problems. Last year, three farmers who had migrated to Niger were captured by a terrorist group. “They were later rescued by our team,” says Mehta.
Nizam Alam is another farmer who left Kannauj in Uttar Pradesh and migrated to Delhi. From being a producer, he has become a seller of fruits in Old Delhi’s Jama Masjid.
Sharing a cramped flat with other migrant workers for Rs.8,000 a month, he sends home whatever little remains. “My family still survives on farming, but it was never enough to meet our needs. Bigger cities provide better opportunities and wages,” he says.
For men like Jiyalal, Purab, Girija, Naushad, Nizam, and many others, giving up farming is less a choice than a last resort, an act of survival. For the women who are left on farms, it is a struggle to move on without any monetary reward for their labour.
Caught between two worlds
They are caught between two challenging worlds: one of villages that offer shelter but not sustenance, and another of cities that provide food but no home. This puts the policies being implemented into question. Mehta said: “Even if the government provides the latest technology at a subsidised rate, the lack of awareness and education becomes a hurdle, since the process involves a tedious application process. Many of the farmers can’t do it due to lack of education.
“Hence, even if there are policies, the ones for whom they are made can’t be reached. Moreover, the government needs to bring uniformity in the pattern of the allocation of these resources to maximise the impact.”
As the migration continues, the question of who will feed the country becomes more prominent. “I’ve given up farming, and now I have no plans of leaving [the city],” says Jiyalal.
The stories of migrants like Jiyalal reflect a larger truth about the country: as the climate grows harsher and government policies fail to protect them, farmers are being uprooted not just from their lands, but from a way of life that once defined the nation.
Abeer Athar is a Delhi-based author and freelance multimedia journalist. He has previously worked in radio broadcasting and editorial roles and has written on a range of social, cultural, and contemporary issues.

This week, 25 Indian startups raised $303.7 million across five growth-stage deals, 16 early-stage deals and three undisclosed rounds. The week also saw seven key hires, four mergers and acquisitions, two startup shutdowns and 250 layoffs.
In contrast, 24 startups had collectively secured about $218.7 million in the previous week.

india-deep-tech-cf432ea046.headline: Semiconductor startup Makr Microsystems raises Rs 10.2 crore for chip inspection technology
india-deep-tech-cf432ea046.fulltext:
Makr Microsystems, a semiconductor metrology startup, has raised Rs 10.2 crore in a seed funding round led by Bluehill VC, a venture capital fund focused on frontier technology.
Artha Venture Fund also participated in the round.
The startup said the funds will go towards further technology development, validating the product with customers, and moving closer to commercial deployment.
As chips have become smaller and more complex, a lot of what actually matters inside them has moved below the surface. Advanced packaging, chiplets, and 3D chip architectures now depend on interfaces and connections that sit buried under several layers of material. Being able to see and measure these hidden structures matters a great deal, since it helps manufacturers understand how a chip was actually built, catch defects, and improve yield.
The tools available for this today are already fairly advanced, but each comes with some compromise. Depending on the technique used, engineers have to trade off between resolution, how deep they can see, how fast the measurement is, and whether the chip sample gets damaged in the process.
Makr is developing a new approach aimed at high resolution, non-destructive subsurface measurement.
The startup's core technology is called Acoustic Atomic Force Microscopy, or AAFM. In simple terms, it combines atomic force microscopy with acoustic sensing, using acoustic signals to gather information beneath the surface that conventional surface based techniques can struggle to access.
Makr is turning this into a platform meant for high resolution, non-destructive inspection of what lies beneath a chip's surface. It is currently targeting use cases such as advanced packaging, hybrid bonding, buried interfaces, chiplet interconnects, and defect detection.
"Semiconductor manufacturing is creating structures that are increasingly difficult to see and measure. As architectures move into the third dimension, understanding what is happening beneath the surface becomes critical to improving yield. Our goal is to make the subsurface measurable, non-destructively and at the resolution the next generation of chipmaking demands," said founder Ashwin Lal.
Ashwin Lal holds a Master's in Physics from IIT Kanpur and a PhD in Microtechnology from EPFL. He had earlier founded Shilps Sciences and worked as an engineer at Applied Materials.
Manu Iyer, General Partner at Bluehill VC, said, "We are excited about companies that sit deeper in critical technology value chains. Makr is solving a difficult problem in semiconductor manufacturing at a time when the industry is moving toward increasingly complex architectures. We believe this is a global opportunity, and that world-class semiconductor equipment and technology can be built from India."

global-economics-a39b7624fa.headline: US added 162,000 jobs in August, with unemployment rate holding steady
global-economics-a39b7624fa.fulltext:
The US economy added 162,000 jobs in August, an uptick after a sluggish summer for the labor market.
The unemployment rate held steady at 4.1%, still down from its most recent peak of 4.5% last November, according to new data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). Despite the relative stability of the unemployment rate, the number of new jobs added to the economy has been fluctuating, going from 214,000 in March down to a 21,000 gain in July and then back up in August.
Figures for job growth in June and July were both revised up. After revisions, job growth in June was 31,000 jobs, up from an initial 20,000, and July was revised up by 44,000 jobs, from an initially reported loss of 23,000 to a gain of 21,000.
Economists had predicted gains would be at least 50,000 new jobs. Earlier in the week, the payroll firm ADP reported private companies added 38,000 jobs in August, lower than initial expectations and the lowest month for new jobs since January. Meanwhile, outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas reported that layoffs have been going down and are 41% lower than cuts that were announced by this time last year.
Economists have pointed out that the labor market appears to be stalled in a “slow hire, slow fire” state, with neither growth nor contractions in jobs.
A separate BLS report from earlier this week showed job openings and layoffs had changed little in July. The number of people quitting their jobs also remained flat, suggesting workers are feeling less confident about their ability to find another job.
For many Americans feeling frustrated about the economy, a lackluster job market feels especially painful when paired with rising prices. US inflation has increased significantly since the start of the war with Iran, with the annual inflation rate going from 2.4% in February to 3.4% in July. In May, price increases reached 4.2%, the highest rate since 2023.
In recent weeks, persistent inflation has started to have a domino effect in the US economy after a sell-off in the US bond market. Yields for US Treasury bonds have been going up since the start of the Iran war, suggesting that investors are concerned about the long-term health of the economy. Higher yields could push up the price of loans, including mortgages, car loans and the interest rate on student debt, making things even more costly for Americans.
Economists are expecting at least one interest rate hike from the US Federal Reserve before the end of the year. Higher interest rates could help lower inflation, but at the risk of destabilizing the labor market.
Last week, Kevin Warsh, the Fed chair, gave his debut speech at the Fed’s symposium in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, where he said the Fed was still committed to getting inflation down to its 2% target rate, but held off on making any firm suggestions on the central bank’s next move.
“We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed,” he said. “Otherwise, we have work to do.”
Donald Trump on Friday celebrated the new job figures and threatened to “stop trading with countries with which we have a deficit” if the Fed doesn’t lower interest rates.
“A STRONG COUNTRY MEANS A LOWER INTEREST RATE –IT’S A BETTER CREDIT… Very simple!” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “We should have the LOWEST RATE of any country in the World, like ‘the old days’.”

global-economics-fddb970953.headline: Trump wants Kevin Warsh to cut rates, markets bet on a hike: Fed chief faces first big test | Explained
global-economics-fddb970953.fulltext:
Sanchari Ghosh Updated5 Sep 2026, 08:35 PM IST Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh faces his first major test, caught between President Donald Trump’s demand for lower interest rates and growing market expectations that the central bank might need to raise rates later this month. Trump on Friday resumes his pressure tactics on the US central bank, calling on the Fed to lower rates following a stronger-than-expected jobs report. “Lower the interest rates because the U.S.A. is a much stronger credit than it was just a short time ago!” Trump said in a social media post. “The Fed Board, with its great new leader, must get smart - BE PATRIOTS for a change.” Trump's intervention adds a political dimension to a Fed policy decision that officials have been closely tying to incoming economic data, particularly inflation. The President had routinely attacked the previous chair, Jerome Powell, over the bank’s policy decisions, but reasonably pulled back the pressure campaign against the Fed after Warsh took over. Friday's message shows that he is now running out of patience. The US jobs report showed nonfarm payrolls increased 162,000 last month and July’s job losses were revised away, suggesting the labour market has more momentum than previously thought. But analysts say the report alone is unlikely to determine the Fed’s next move, with the central bank’s decision expected to hinge largely on next week’s inflation data. “Today’s data lends support to the hawkish camp, but stops shy of making a definitive case for a rate hike on September 16,” Vail Hartman, a strategist at BMO Capital Markets, wrote. “While the market-implied probability of a rate hike this month has increased, the employment data will play a secondary role to inflation.” That puts next week’s inflation readings firmly in focus. The Bureau of Labor Statistics will release August data for the producer price index on Thursday, followed by the consumer price index on Friday. Olu Sonola, head of US economics at Fitch Rating, described the jobs report as “unequivocally strong”, but said: “The real event risk is next week’s CPI report. That is the print capable of moving the needle.” In a similar note, Mark Spindel, chief investment officer at Potomac River Capital LLC told Bloomberg, today’s jobs report corrected some of the previous weakness in the employment data, particularly in sectors like public schools. “As strong as today’s data was, I don’t think anyone will be triggered to tighten on today’s data alone,” he said. “Next week’s inflation report will be determinative.” With Fed officials concerned about persistently high inflation but divided over how monetary policy should respond in the near term, new evidence of price pressures could tilt the Federal Open Market Committee toward a rate hike. Three policymakers dissented at the July meeting in favour of a quarter-point hike, while Governor Christopher Waller said during a Reuters event that he is inclined to hold rates unless the inflation data comes in “hot.” For Warsh, the dilemma is particularly significant. So far, the new Fed chief has talked tough on inflation, but has pointedly avoided any specific hints that he favours a rate increase in the coming months. At Jackson Hole last week, Warsh said policymakers must be confident inflation is meaningfully slowing, otherwise they had “work to do.” The decision could therefore become Warsh’s first major test of how he balances economic data, market expectations and growing political pressure from the White House. Ukraine war: how escalating attacks are upending lives in Kyiv
Russia is now using more jet-powered drones, which are faster and harder for Ukraine to intercept than propeller-powered models
Commuters stranded; children rushed underground in the middle of the school day; festivals cancelled; walks punctuated by booming air defences. Near-constant drone attacks are the stark new reality in Kyiv, and daily life is likely to get harder.
Kyiv has survived many traumas since Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Despite the initial shock of war and the advent of attack drones and ballistic missiles, residents adapted and managed to impose a semblance of normality.
But as a fifth full winter of war approaches, that is becoming harder to maintain.
Over the summer, Moscow began sending swarms of high-speed, jet-propelled drones that are more destructive and harder to shoot down than older propeller-powered models.
For the last 10 days, air attacks have been around-the-clock rather than mainly at night, puncturing Ukrainians’ sense that their country’s own long-range drone campaign against Russia was swinging the war back in their favour.

other-interests-c291e4fc75.headline: Marine conservation collides with mining in Indonesia’s biodiversity-rich Moramo Bay
other-interests-c291e4fc75.fulltext:
- Pressure on a protected marine area in Indonesia’s Southeast Sulawesi province is growing as conservation efforts intersect with mining activity.
- Moramo Bay is part of the Coral Triangle, one of the world’s richest marine biodiversity regions, and provides habitat for humphead wrasse and other protected species.
- Researchers and officials say the health of its coral reefs and marine life is increasingly under scrutiny as development expands around the conservation area.
SOUTH KONAWE, Indonesia — A marine protected area in Indonesia’s Southeast Sulawesi province is home to a critically depleted population of humphead wrasse. The species presence helped the area gain its protected status, but mining permits overlap parts of the conservation zone and line its coast.
A 2024 government survey, published the following year, found just 22 humphead wrasse (Cheilinus undulatus) across 10 sampling stations — an average density of 1.17 fish per hectare — in the Moramo Bay local marine protected area (LMPA) in Southeast Sulawesi’s South Konawe district. It recorded no fish at three sites where the species was still observed in 2018.
Officials and researchers say the bay’s coral reefs face mounting pressure from sedimentation, pollution, vessel activity and other threats, but no study has established a direct link between mining and the wrasse’s decline.
“In a polluted area … this fish will definitely disappear,” Sasanti Retno Suharti, a coral reef fish ecology researcher who has been researching humphead wrasse since 2006, told Mongabay Indonesia in August. “It will move far away into deeper waters.”
“If it is no longer there, eventually the crown-of-thorns starfish will take over and feed on the corals,” she added. “The ecosystem will be damaged.”
The presence of humphead wrasse was one reason Southeast Sulawesi first proposed Moramo Bay as a LMPA in 2011. The proposed area expanded to 21,786 hectares (53,834 acres) in 2016 from 10,371 hectares (25,627 acres) in 2014. In 2021, the Ministry of Marine Affairs and Fisheries designated Moramo Bay and surrounding islands as a 21,902-hectare conservation area spanning parts of South Konawe, Konawe regencies and the coastal city of Kendari.
The designation was intended to protect coral reefs, seagrass meadows, mangroves and protected fish species, including the humphead wrasse, said Anung Wijaya, a conservation analyst at the Southeast Sulawesi Marine and Fisheries Agency. The waters lie west of the Banda Sea within the Coral Triangle, a region known as “the Amazon of the Seas” for its rich marine biodiversity.
A 2024 study led by Anung, however, found a 12.6% decline in coral cover between 2018 and 2024 on the waters off Lara Island, where the humphead wrasse is now virtually extinct and where coral bleaching linked to global warming has exacerbated decline in coral cover there. His study warned that ongoing limestone mining in Wawatu, a village on the mainland, could affect coral reefs around Lara Island, which is less than 2 km from the mining area, through sedimentation and reduced water quality.
“Reclamation activities to build infrastructure supporting mining operations, such as special terminals, as well as the transportation of processed mining materials, can contribute to increased water turbidity in the surrounding area,” Anung writes in his study.
Anung told Mongabay Indonesia that no study had established a direct link between mining and the decline in the humphead wrasse population in Moramo Bay. “If we talk about the connection, it is possible,” he said, adding that his agency can only convey its findings to government agencies responsible for mining.
The humphead wrasse, one of the largest reef fish in the Coral Triangle, plays an important role in maintaining healthy coral reef ecosystems by feeding on a range of reef organisms, including crown-of-thorns starfish (Acanthaster planci). In Indonesia, where the humphead wrasse is protected based on its size, its presence is also considered to be an indicator of a relatively healthy reef habitat, while declining numbers can signal broader degradation of coral reef ecosystems.
Jupri, a marine and coastal ecosystem manager at the Denpasar Marine Management Agency’s Southeast Sulawesi working area, also raised concerns about nickel mining upstream of the Wandaeha River, which flows into Moramo Bay. Agency observations found sedimentation, coral reef damage and water visibility of less than 10 meters (33 feet) around Gala and Woru-woru islands near the river mouth.
“The Wandaeha area used to be a producer of ebi [baby shrimp],” he said. “There is no longer any ebi production because of mining operations on land.” Land within the conservation area should also be protected from mining as it is a habitat for sea bamboo (Isis hippuris) and sea turtles, he added.
Jupri said a production permit for Class C quarry materials, such as limestone and construction stone, is also located opposite Lara Island, although operations have not started.
“If this mining begins operating, we don’t know what the future of the Moramo Bay LMPA will look like,” he said.
At least 12 mining permit areas for Class C quarry materials are located along the Moramo Bay coast, not counting a nickel mine upstream of the Wandaeha River and nearby shipyards and special terminals. Mining permit areas for Class C construction materials, such as limestone and other quarry materials, also overlap the conservation area, according to a comparison of zoning data from the marine affairs ministry and the Energy and Mineral Resources Ministry’s ESDM One Map Indonesia.
“Ideally, if it is a conservation area, there should not be any mining industry around it,” Jupri said, adding that he had reported findings on potential threats from mining to the Southeast Sulawesi Marine and Fisheries Agency.
Three companies have production operation permits for quarry materials, while the others remain at the reservation or exploration stage. The three companies are PT Citra Khusuma Sultra (CKS), PT Ramadhan Moramo Raya (RMR; also formerly known as CV Ramadhan Moramo) and PT Hoffmen Energi Perkasa (HEP). HEP borders the Moramo Bay LMPA, while the permits held by CKS and RMR extend into the sea and overlap the conservation area.
Muhammad Hasbullah Idris, head of the minerals and coal division at the Southeast Sulawesi Energy and Mineral Resources Agency, said the permits predated the designation of the conservation area.
“These are old mining permits,” Hasbullah told Mongabay Indonesia in July. “Before they were issued, we would certainly have requested confirmation of their conformity with the spatial plan from the regency government. The regency government declared the areas suitable for mining.”
CKS and RMR received mining permits in 2015 for 122 hectares and 11 hectares, respectively, and later secured extensions to operate through 2030. Hasbullah said the permits were issued under South Konawe Regional Regulation No. 19/2013, which set the district’s 2013-2033 spatial plan. Meanwhile, HEP received an exploration permit in 2023 and a production permit covering 11 hectares from 2026 to 2031.
Hasbullah said he visited the mining sites with other government agencies in February to check for signs of pollution entering the conservation area. “When we went down there, we could still see that the water was clear. I went there in February, and it was still clear,” he said.
Some mining permits, however, cover marine areas and tourist destinations that should be off-limits to mining under South Konawe Regional Regulation No. 5/2020 on the 2020-2040 spatial plan, which revoked the earlier 2013 regulation.
Hasbullah said no mining would take place in those areas, “That’s why it became controversial later on, when it turned out to be a tourist destination.”
Andi Rahman, executive director of the Southeast Sulawesi chapter of the Indonesian Forum for the Environment (Walhi), the country’s biggest green NGO, criticized the extension of mining permits that overlap the Moramo Bay LMPA.
He also questioned the Southeast Sulawesi Energy and Mineral Resources Agency’s claim that there had been no pollution in waters around the mining sites, saying the assessment was not based on standardized indicators.
“Our question is, if the area is damaged and polluted, who will be held responsible? For the past two years, we have been calling for an evaluation while the permits had not yet expired,” Andi told Mongabay Indonesia in August.
According to Andi, the issuance and extension of the permits did not take into account coastal and small-island spatial planning aimed at protecting marine species. He said the government should have reviewed the permits after South Konawe revised its spatial plan.
“If the reason is that the permits had already been issued, fine,” he said. “But when the spatial plan changes, that should be grounds for evaluating and revoking the mining permits.”
This story was first published here on August 30, 2026.
Basten Gokkon, senior staff writer for Indonesia at Mongabay, adapted this reporting.
